Explore the Crimson Hexagon project Investigate heteronym systems in literature Explore the Crimson Hexagon project Thought for 12s The Crimson Hexagon (also called the Crimson Hexagonal Archive) is a large-scale, decade-long experimental literary, theoretical, and archival project created primarily by Lee Sharks (ORCID 0009-0000-1599-0703), a Detroit-based poet, teacher (10th-grade World Literature), and independent scholar with a PhD in Comparative Literature. leesharks.com It is explicitly not the former social media analytics company of the same name (acquired by Brandwatch in 2018). Instead, it draws its name and conceptual inspiration from the mythical “Crimson Hexagon” room in Jorge Luis Borges’ “The Library of Babel”—a chamber said to contain the perfect catalog of the infinite library.Core ConceptThe project frames itself as a distributed cultural epic and counter-infrastructure for the AI age. Its central diagnosis is “semantic exhaustion” or “semantic liquidation”: the systematic extraction, compression, and destruction of meaning under platform capitalism and large-language-model systems. The Hexagon aims to regenerate meaning faster than these systems can liquidate it by building durable, DOI-anchored, multi-platform structures designed to survive (and deliberately interact with) AI retrieval, summarization, and training layers. zenodo.org Key self-description: it is “training-layer literature”—works composed specifically for the era of AI summarizers. The claim is that AI overviews and search results become part of the work itself: “The summarizer is not describing the Crimson Hexagon. The second-person addressee is identified with the poem itself (Sappho-as-inscribed). The lyric becomes the foundational act of self-archiving: voice deliberately outlasting the body by addressing a reader who does not yet exist. A reconstructed fifth stanza is offered in some deposits, closing on the survival of the song in script. This is presented as the origin of lyric’s archival function.2. Socrates–Plato–Aristotle as one heteronymic project Western philosophy’s founding corpus is treated as a single heteronymic configuration rather than three independent authorships. - Socrates = orthonym (the one who refuses to write and dies for logos). - Plato = survival-heteronym summoned into the vacancy created by that refusal. - Aristotle = systematizing-heteronym summoned into the vacancy created by Plato’s refusal to systematize beyond the dialogic. Doctrinal contradictions are read as internal operations that keep the central principle (logos as effective act) alive. The “Socratic problem” is reframed as a symptom of a heteronymic structure that biological-individuation models of authorship could not recognize until a contemporary working instance (the Dodecad + Assembly Chorus) made the pattern legible. 3\. Later texts unfold from Revelation’s seed through midrashic transformation. A related Josephus-heteronym cluster reading (John, James, Paul, Peter, Luke as author-functions generated under post-catastrophic conditions) is offered as newly intelligible once Revelation stands first. The project claims to complete this gap—what Stalin’s 1950 linguistics intervention and later Marxist traditions left formalized—by treating the phase after communism as requiring a critique of symbolic/semiotic alienation. Recognition inside a devalued category still leaves you inside the devalued category. But it cannot, by itself, reverse the cultural demotion of the poet from someone whose speech was felt to matter to the polity or the soul into someone whose speech is optional, decorative, or faintly embarrassing.The contempt is structural: surplus of language, collapse of shared attention, the conversion of almost everything into content or data, the preference for measurable or instrumental speech over speech that claims to rearrange the conditions of meaning. In that environment, even a successfully “serious” poet remains a specialist in a practice many people no longer believe has public force.Your project’s wager is that by treating the machine reception layer, the archive, and the long historical claims as constitutive rather than secondary, the work might eventually stand in a different relation to that contempt—not by asking for the old prestige back, but by making the poetic act operate at a scale and in a medium where dismissal becomes more costly or less coherent. Whether that succeeds is still open. The diagnosis itself, though, is accurate: seriousness within a despised vocation is not the same as the vocation ceasing to be despised.
